k-11.7-monitor-risks-tools.title: 11.7 Monitor Risks (continued): technical performance analysis, reserve analysis, risk audits, risk reviews, outputs
k-11.7-monitor-risks-tools.notes: Inputs continued: work performance data (responses implemented, risks occurred, active and closed); work performance reports (variance analysis, earned value and forecasting data - relevant for performance-related risks). Tools: data analysis - technical performance analysis (compare technical accomplishments with the schedule of technical achievement using objective, quantifiable measures such as weight, transaction times, number of delivered defects, storage capacity; deviation can indicate threats or opportunities), reserve analysis (compare remaining contingency reserves with remaining risk to judge adequacy; may be shown as a burndown chart); audits - risk audits assess the effectiveness of the risk management process; the PM ensures they happen at the frequency in the risk management plan; may be part of routine reviews, a risk review meeting or separate meetings; format and objectives defined beforehand; meetings - risk reviews (scheduled regularly; examine and document response effectiveness for overall and individual risks; may identify new risks incl. secondary risks, reassess risks, close outdated risks, record issues from occurred risks, capture lessons; part of status meetings or dedicated). Outputs: work performance information (occurred risks compared with expectations - shows effectiveness of response planning and implementation); change requests (incl. recommended corrective and preventive actions for overall or individual risk); plan updates (any component); document updates (assumption log, issue log, lessons learned, risk register - new, outdated, realised risks and updated responses; risk report - status of major risks, overall level, top risks, responses and owners, conclusions, recommendations, risk audit conclusions); OPA updates (templates for the risk management plan, risk register and risk report; risk breakdown structure).

p-procurement-overview.title: Project Procurement Management overview: three processes, legal nature of contracts, buyer-seller roles, centralised vs decentralised purchasing, trends, tailoring, agile
p-procurement-overview.section: 12 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile (Figure 12-1)
p-procurement-overview.notes: Processes to purchase or acquire products, services or results from outside the project team, including developing and administering agreements - contracts, purchase orders, memoranda of agreement (MOAs), internal service level agreements (SLAs). Authorised procurers may be team members, management or the purchasing department. Processes: 12.1 Plan Procurement Management (document procurement decisions, specify the approach, identify potential sellers); 12.2 Conduct Procurements (obtain seller responses, select a seller, award a contract); 12.3 Control Procurements (manage procurement relationships, monitor contract performance, make changes and corrections, close out contracts). Written from the buyer's viewpoint. Key concepts: significant legal obligations and penalties; the PM need not be a procurement-law expert but must know enough to decide intelligently, and is typically not authorised to sign legal agreements binding the organisation. Agreements describe a buyer-seller relationship, from labour hours at a rate to multiyear international construction contracts; the approach should match complexity and comply with laws. A contract should clearly state expected deliverables and results incl. knowledge transfer; anything not in the contract cannot be legally enforced; culture and local law affect enforceability internationally. A purchasing contract has terms and conditions; the PM team ensures procurements meet project needs while the procurement office ensures policy compliance. Agreement forms: contract, SLA, understanding, MOA, purchase order. Contracts get more extensive approval, often by legal, to ensure the products/services are adequately described and legal; legal terms often sit in standardised appendices. Complex projects may manage multiple contracts simultaneously or in sequence, each with its own life cycle. Seller names: contractor, vendor, service provider, supplier; buyer names: owner, subcontractor, acquiring organisation, service requestor, purchaser; the seller is first a bidder, then the selected source, then the contracted supplier. The winning seller may manage its work as a project: the buyer becomes its key customer/stakeholder; contract terms and the procurement statement of work (also called technical SOW) become key inputs and may constrain options (e.g., buyer approval of staffing); the seller may itself buy from lower tiers. The seller may be internal but external to the project and may join an integrated team after award. Decentralised purchasing: in small organisations without a procurement department the PM may negotiate and sign; centralised purchasing: a separate department purchases, negotiates and signs. International contracts state the legal jurisdiction. Trends: advances in tools (online procurement portals; building information model - BIM - in construction saves time and money and reduces claims; increasingly mandated); more advanced risk management (contracts allocate specific risks to the parties best able to manage them; buyer accepts risks contractors can't control - corporate policy and regulatory changes; contracts may require risk management); changing contracting processes (growth of multibillion-dollar megaprojects with international contractors; contractor works with the client on procurement for quantity discounts; internationally recognised standard contract forms to reduce claims); logistics and supply chain management (long-lead items drive schedule - 2 to 3 months in IT, 1 to 2 years or more in complex construction; may be procured early from top-level design; primary and backup sources; local-content purchase requirements); technology and stakeholder relations (site webcams for public projects improve communication and reduce disputes); trial engagements (paid initial work with several candidate sellers before committing). Tailoring: complexity of procurement (one or many), physical location, governance and regulatory environment (laws and auditing), availability of contractors. Agile: specific sellers may extend the team in a collaborative, shared-risk-and-reward model; large projects may combine adaptive and stable parts under a master services agreement (MSA) with adaptive work in an appendix or supplement so it can change without affecting the overall contract. ITTOs for 12.1-12.3 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 12-1.

p-12.1-plan-procurement.title: 12.1 Plan Procurement Management: typical procurement steps, contract types, make-or-buy, source selection methods, procurement strategy, bid documents, SOW/TOR, source selection criteria, independent estimates
p-12.1-plan-procurement.notes: Document procurement decisions, specify the approach and identify potential sellers; key benefit: determines whether to acquire from outside and, if so, what, how and when (from other parts of the organisation or external sources); once or at predefined points. Define procurement roles early and staff the team with procurement expertise; participants may include purchasing and legal; document responsibilities in the plan. Typical steps: prepare the procurement SOW or terms of reference (TOR); prepare a high-level cost estimate for the budget; advertise; short-list qualified sellers; prepare and issue bid documents; sellers prepare and submit proposals; technical evaluation incl. quality; cost evaluation; final combined quality and cost evaluation to select the winner; finalise negotiations and sign. Schedule requirements influence the strategy, and procurement decisions affect the schedule (integrated with Develop Schedule, Estimate Activity Resources and make-or-buy). Inputs: charter (objectives, description, summary milestones, preapproved financial resources); business documents (business case alignment; benefits management plan drives procurement dates and contract language); plan (scope management plan - managing contractor scope; quality management plan - standards and codes for RFPs, prequalification, selection; resource management plan - what is purchased or leased; scope baseline - known scope elements form the SOW/TOR); documents (milestone list - when sellers must deliver; project team assignments - procurement skills and availability; requirements documentation - technical requirements and those with contractual/legal implications: health, safety, security, performance, environmental, insurance, intellectual property, equal employment, licences, permits; RTM; resource requirements; risk register - some risks are transferred via agreements; stakeholder register - incl. regulators, contracting and legal personnel); EEFs (marketplace conditions and available products; sellers' past performance and reputation; typical terms and conditions; unique local requirements such as local labour or sellers; legal advice; contract management systems incl. contract change control; multi-tier prequalified supplier systems; financial accounting and payment systems); OPAs (preapproved seller lists; formal procurement policies; contract types). Contract types - two broad families plus a hybrid: fixed-price (use when requirements are well defined and no significant scope change is expected): firm fixed price (FFP - most common, favoured by buyers; price set at the outset, changes only with scope changes); fixed price incentive fee (FPIF - financial incentives tied to cost, schedule or technical performance metrics; a price ceiling is set and all costs above it are the seller's responsibility); fixed price with economic price adjustments (FPEPA - for multi-year performance or payments in another currency; predefined adjustments for changed conditions such as inflation or commodity cost changes). Cost-reimbursable (use when scope is expected to change significantly; seller reimbursed for legitimate actual costs plus a fee as profit): cost plus fixed fee (CPFF - fixed fee calculated as a percentage of initial estimated costs; changes only with scope changes); cost plus incentive fee (CPIF - predetermined incentive fee for meeting performance objectives; cost overruns or underruns versus target shared by a prenegotiated formula, e.g., 80/20); cost plus award fee (CPAF - most of the fee earned against broad subjective criteria judged solely by the buyer, generally not appealable). Time and material (T&M, also 'time and means') - hybrid of cost-reimbursable and fixed-price; staff augmentation, experts, outside support when a precise SOW can't be quickly written. Types are often combined in practice. Tools: expert judgment (procurement, contract types and documents, regulations); market research (industry and seller capabilities; conferences, online reviews; refine objectives to leverage maturing technologies while balancing seller-base risk); make-or-buy analysis (factors: current resource allocation and skills, need for specialised or independent expertise, desire not to expand permanent employment, risks; may use payback period, ROI, IRR, discounted cash flow, NPV, benefit/cost analysis); source selection analysis (review prioritisation of competing demands first; publish the evaluation method in procurement documents; methods: least cost - standard/routine work with well-defined outcomes; qualifications only - small-value procurements, choose from a short list by credibility, qualifications, experience, references; quality-based/highest technical proposal score - rank technical proposals, negotiate with the top one if its financial proposal is acceptable; quality and cost-based - cost included, quality weighted higher when risk/uncertainty is greater; sole source - one seller asked for proposals, acceptable only when justified, an exception; fixed budget - budget disclosed in the RFP, best technical proposal within it; only when the SOW is precise, no changes anticipated and the budget cannot be exceeded); meetings (information exchange with potential bidders for a mutually beneficial approach; strategy for managing and monitoring the procurement). Outputs: procurement management plan (international/national/local competitive bidding; align external financing with the plan and schedule; coordination with scheduling processes; timetable; procurement metrics; roles and authority vs procurement department; constraints and assumptions; legal jurisdiction and payment currency; whether independent estimates are used as evaluation criteria; risk issues such as performance bonds or insurance; prequalified sellers); procurement strategy (after make-or-buy: delivery method - professional services: buyer/services provider with or without subcontracting, joint venture, provider as representative; industrial/commercial construction: turnkey, design build (DB), design bid build (DBB), design build operate (DBO), build own operate transfer (BOOT); contract payment types separate from delivery methods: lump sum, FFP, CPAF, CPIF, T&M, target cost; fixed-price for predictable well-defined work, cost plus for evolving work, incentives and awards to align objectives; procurement phases - sequencing and objectives, performance indicators and milestones, phase transition criteria, monitoring and evaluation plan, knowledge transfer); bid documents (bid/tender/quotation when selection is price-based; proposal when technical capability or approach matters most; request for information (RFI - more information about the goods/services needed, typically followed by RFQ or RFP); request for quotation (RFQ - how vendors would meet requirements and/or how much it will cost); request for proposal (RFP - when there is a problem whose solution is not easy to determine; most formal, strict rules on content, timeline and responses); documents describe the desired response form, the SOW and contractual provisions; detail consistent with value and risk; detailed enough for consistent responses yet flexible for seller suggestions); procurement statement of work (developed from the scope baseline; only the portion of scope in that contract; enough detail for sellers to judge capability - specifications, quantity, quality levels, performance data, period of performance, work location; clear, complete, concise; includes collateral services such as performance reporting or post-project support; revised until incorporated into a signed agreement); terms of reference (TOR, for services: tasks and coordination requirements, applicable standards, data to submit for approval, data and services the buyer will provide, schedule for initial submission and review/approval time); source selection criteria (capability and capacity; product and life-cycle cost; delivery dates; technical expertise and approach; relevant experience; adequacy of approach and work plan; key staff qualifications, availability and competence; financial stability; management experience; knowledge transfer and training; for international projects 'local content'; expressed as scores, colour codes or descriptions in a weighting system to select a seller or rank proposals for a negotiating sequence); make-or-buy decisions; independent cost estimates (own or outside professional estimate as a benchmark; significant differences may mean a deficient or ambiguous SOW or that sellers misunderstood or failed to respond fully); change requests.
